questions.question: Describe the core-periphery model — core, periphery, backwash, spread and cumulative causation — and apply it to South Africa at national scale.
questions.expected_answer: The model says development organises space into a powerful core, where economic activity, investment, skills and political power concentrate, and a dependent periphery that supplies the core with raw materials and labour while receiving little in return. Its engine is cumulative causation: success attracts success, as each new factory draws suppliers, workers and taxes that fund infrastructure and attract further investment. The backwash effect is the drain of the periphery's young, skilled people and capital toward the core, which weakens the periphery's ability to catch up; spread effects are the smaller counter-flows of investment, remittances and demand from core to periphery. Nationally, Gauteng is South Africa's core — producing roughly a third of GDP on the smallest provincial footprint — while the former homeland districts of the Eastern Cape and Limpopo are periphery, exporting migrant workers to the cities. Apartheid engineered this pattern by law, designing the homelands as labour reservoirs, and post-1994 policies such as the Coega industrial development zone and development corridors are deliberate attempts to build new cores and strengthen spread effects.

questions.question: Outline Rostow's five stages of economic growth and evaluate the model with at least three criticisms.
questions.expected_answer: Rostow's stages run: traditional society, dominated by subsistence farming with little surplus; preconditions for take-off, when commercial farming, railways, ports and banks develop and an entrepreneurial class emerges; take-off, the decisive burst when manufacturing grows rapidly, investment passes roughly 10 per cent of national income and growth becomes self-sustaining; drive to maturity, when industry diversifies and technology spreads economy-wide; and the age of high mass consumption, when most households afford consumer durables and services dominate employment. Criticisms: the model assumes every country follows the Western path drawn from British and American history, ignoring different cultures, resources and choices; it ignores colonialism, since early industrialisers were fuelled partly by colonies whose development was deliberately suppressed; it ignores the core-periphery trap, in which countries locked into exporting raw materials may never accumulate the capital take-off requires — the vicious circle of poverty makes the second step a wall; and it treats mass consumption as the summit with no stage for sustainability. South Africa also shows that one country can occupy several stages at once, and that apartheid deliberately excluded most of the population from the staircase — a history the model cannot represent.

questions.question: Name and explain the five aspects of development, including the exact Brundtland definition of sustainable development and an example of appropriate-scale development.
questions.expected_answer: Economic development is rising production, jobs, income and investment — necessary to fund everything else but not sufficient alone. Social development converts economic gains into better lives: education, health care, housing, safe water and the full inclusion of women. Sustainable development is, in the Brundtland definition, development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs — so exhausting forests or aquifers for short-term GDP is not development but the spending of future generations' inheritance. Appropriate-scale development matches the solution to the community: a remote Karoo village is better served by solar panels and a borehole pump that residents can maintain themselves than by a distant mega-project, which is why the term travels with appropriate technology. Spatial development addresses where development happens, tackling the gap between booming cores and neglected peripheries rather than letting gains pile up in one favoured region.
